statement: Grip type, grip width, and forearm orientation on the lat pulldown meaningfully bias which region of the latissimus dorsi is trained, so a lifter can 'target' the lat differently (e.g., wide vs narrow, pronated vs supinated, neutral) to drive region-specific lat development.
nuance: All three skeptic lenses refute (strength 0.90-0.95). The claim of region-specific LAT development rests entirely on acute surface-EMG proxies, and the one direct study (Brusco, 40 trained men, 7 grip variants at 70% 1RM) found NO significant difference in latissimus dorsi activation across grip type, width, or forearm orientation (LD held ~45-62% MVC regardless) and explicitly states the data 'challenge the assumption that grip targets this muscle.' What actually changes with grip is SYNERGIST loading (posterior delt, biceps, traps) and the small LD-centroid shift seen in the HD-EMG paper -- but a centroid shift is not demonstrated regional hypertrophy, and there is zero volume-equated growth data. Effect vs practical: grip choice meaningfully alters synergist recruitment, comfort, joint safety and leverage (a real reason to vary grips), but it does not steer where the lat grows. The claim conflates 'loads synergists / feels different' with 'grows different lat regions,' and even overstates equivalent activation as differential targeting.
population: resistance-trained men (acute EMG, 70% 1RM); no hypertrophy data

statement: The front (to-chest) lat pulldown produces greater latissimus dorsi recruitment/activation than the behind-the-neck lat pulldown, making it the superior variation for building the lats.
nuance: All three lenses refute (strength 0.88-0.90). 'Superior for building the lats' rests on a single acute HD-EMG study (14 trained men, 8-RM) that is both load-confounded and phase-dependent: the front-LPD condition used ~18% greater absolute load (70.0 vs 59.3 kg) and greater bar displacement, which the authors flag as inflating front-LPD EMG, and the LD advantage appears only in the descending/concentric phase (ES 0.97) while the back-LPD LD is actually higher in the ascending/eccentric phase (ES 0.63) -- a reversal, not a clean win. Prior literature is itself mixed (Sperandei 2009 no difference; Signorile 2002 favored front). Effect vs practical: front-LPD is a defensible default because it permits heavier loading and is safer for most shoulders, and the study authors recommend programming BOTH for varied spatial stimulus -- but there is no hypertrophy data, so the growth-superiority leap is unsupported. 'Greater recruitment' is partly true (one phase, load-confounded); 'superior for building lats' is not established.
population: resistance-trained men (acute HD-EMG, 8-RM); no hypertrophy data

statement: Lengthened partials (reps biased to the stretched portion of the range of motion) produce more muscle growth than full range-of-motion training.
nuance: All three lenses refute the blanket 'more growth than full ROM' as stated (strength 0.72-0.80), but the underlying effect-direction has partial support in the wider literature, so the net verdict is disputed rather than flatly refuted. Two-layer problem: (1) the three cited sources contain NO lengthened-partials-vs-full-ROM data at all (RP/Israetel mentions partials only in passing; Krzysztofik 2019 reviews other techniques; the Sportsmed 2026 NMA does not analyze ROM), so as cited the claim is unsubstantiated. (2) In the broader literature the lenses gesture at (Wolf 2025, Pedrosa, Kassiano, Maeo), training at long muscle lengths tends to match or modestly beat short-length/full-ROM-omitting-the-stretch work, but the effect is SMALL, muscle/region-specific (distal quads, biceps/triceps long head), partly confounded by effort/load and partly in untrained subjects, and tends to vanish against a quality full ROM that already trains the stretch. Effect vs practical: lengthened partials are a reasonable time/volume add-on for lagging regions, not a demonstrated universal upgrade over full-ROM training.
population: mostly trained/recreationally-trained young adults; isolation-exercise and single-muscle regional studies; corpus-cited sources are general technique reviews, not ROM trials

statement: Supersets (back-to-back sets with little rest) compromise hypertrophy relative to traditional straight sets.
nuance: Two lenses refute (strength 0.85) and one survives precisely BECAUSE the rejection is grounded in measured growth, not a proxy. The asserted hypertrophy PENALTY is contradicted exactly where volume is held constant: the volume-matched superset RCT (Burke 2025, n=43 resistance-trained, 8 wk, agonist-antagonist supersets to failure, Bayes factors favoring the null) found the SAME muscle-thickness gains across all assessed muscles plus equal strength/power/endurance/body-comp, while cutting session time 36%. The Sportsmed 2026 NMA had too few superset studies (n=3) to pool but reports no hypertrophy decrement and classes supersets as time-effective; Iversen 2021 shows supersets roughly halve training time while maintaining (or via antagonist preloading, raising) volume. Honest finding: hypertrophy is NOT compromised, it is equivalent, provided weekly volume is preserved. Legitimate caveats the claim inflates: agonist/same-muscle supersets acutely cut reps/volume per session (must be made up), and supersets raise acute fatigue/lactate/RPE needing more recovery -- fatigue/volume-management cautions, not a chronic growth penalty for the common antagonist superset.
population: resistance-trained young men and women (Burke RCT); NMA pooled untrained-to-moderately-trained healthy adults; agonist-antagonist/different-muscle supersets to failure, 8 wk

statement: Pre-exhaustion supersets (isolation move immediately before a compound for the same muscle) increase target-muscle activation and hypertrophy versus normal exercise order.
nuance: All three lenses refute (strength 0.85-0.90) and both prongs of the claim fail. Activation: EMG does not support increased target-muscle activation in the subsequent compound -- Fujita 2022 is literally titled '...Does Not Increase Muscle Activity in Target Muscle...' and Golas (in Krzysztofik 2019) found a pre-exhaust fly did not raise pectoralis-major activity in the following bench and instead raised synergists (triceps/anterior delt), the opposite of the intended rationale; the activation prong also leans on an untrained-subject study. Hypertrophy: the only chronic pre-exhaustion trial pooled (Fisher 2014) showed no growth difference vs traditional order, and the whole advanced-paradigm class was equivalent (SMD ~0.00). Effect vs practical: pre-exhaustion reliably REDUCES reps/load in the following compound (lowering effective compound volume) rather than raising stimulus. No volume-/effort-equated evidence supports either increased prime-mover activation or growth. Evidence base is thin (small acute EMG studies plus one chronic RCT in a meta), so direction is moderate-high confidence but not heavily replicated.
population: untrained and recreationally trained adults (18-45y); acute EMG work in both untrained and trained men, chronic data only in a single PE RCT pooled in a trained-population meta-analysis

statement: Advanced set-intensity techniques as a class (drop sets, rest-pause, supersets, pyramids, cluster sets) produce greater muscle hypertrophy than volume-equated traditional straight-set training.
nuance: All three lenses refute the SUPERIORITY assertion (strength 0.85-0.96), but the honest finding is no meaningful hypertrophy difference at matched volume -- the claim overstates equivalence as superiority, so the directed verdict is equivalent. Three meta-analyses converge: Fonseca 2023 (trained, drop-sets/rest-pause/supersets/pyramids/GVT/eccentric/super-slow/pre-exhaust vs traditional) all-measures SMD = -0.00 (95% CI -0.15 to 0.14, I2=0%, GRADE moderate); Tsartsapakis 2026 (recreationally trained) hypertrophy g = 0.046 (p=0.370, NS); Sports Medicine 2026 Bayesian NMA found no method consistently superior for hypertrophy. This is the classic non-equation error -- claimed superiority over volume-equated straight sets is directly contradicted. Effect vs practical: when volume is equated, growth is equivalent; the legitimate reasons to use these techniques are a moderate STRENGTH edge (Tsartsapakis g=0.351, driven by rest-pause/VBT/eccentric), TIME-EFFICIENCY/training density, and variety/plateau-breaking -- none of which is 'more growth at matched volume.'
population: healthy recreationally/resistance-trained adults ~18-50y (Fonseca: trained; Tsartsapakis: recreationally trained 18-45y; Sports Med NMA: untrained-to-moderately-trained)

statement: More weekly volume always means more muscle growth: hypertrophy increases monotonically with weekly set volume, so adding sets keeps adding growth (commonly stretched to 'just keep adding sets to grow more').
nuance: Lenses split (2 refute at 0.70-0.82, 1 survives at 0.20): a genuine positive dose-response exists, but the absolutist 'always / keeps adding' overstates it. Supported core (outcome data): Pelland 2026 meta-regression (67 studies, 2,058 participants) found 100% posterior probability that the volume->hypertrophy slope exceeds zero, with no plateau detected within the studied range, and SBS argues growth keeps rising past ~25 (possibly 45) weekly sets. Overstated part: (1) both best-fit models show DIMINISHING RETURNS, so 'keeps adding growth' in a naive linear sense is false; (2) volume-equated comparisons show no further benefit beyond ~12-20 sets/muscle/week for quads (p=0.19) and biceps (p=0.59) in Baz-Valle 2022 (only triceps benefited from >20); (3) the relationship cannot be monotone forever -- an inverted-U is assumed at high volume, just not yet located. Effect vs practical: volume is a real progressive-overload lever, but the accurate statement is 'more volume tends to mean more growth WITH diminishing returns up to a still-uncertain ceiling,' not 'always more.'
population: trained and untrained young-to-middle-aged adults (Pelland: 79% male, mean age ~25y; Baz-Valle: trained men 18-35y)

statement: There is a per-week 'junk-volume' ceiling for hypertrophy (roughly ~5 hard sets per muscle per session, or an MRV around ~10-20 sets/week) beyond which additional sets stop producing any extra growth and become wasted 'junk volume.'
nuance: All three lenses refute the load-bearing per-WEEK ceiling (strength 0.60-0.75), but the claim mixes one defensible idea with one unsupported one, so the net verdict is disputed. Defensible part (per-SESSION diminishing returns): Krieger/Weightology synthesizes acute MPS and per-session data showing within-session hypertrophy plateaus near ~8 sets (long rest) or ~15-16 sets (short rest) -- a reasonable per-session 'junk volume' basis and the rationale for spreading weekly volume across more sessions. Unsupported part (a hard per-WEEK MRV ~10-20): Pelland 2026 detected NO weekly plateau (positive slope, diminishing but not vanishing); SBS argues the weekly limit exceeds 25 and possibly 45 sets, capping above ~25 only for data sparsity; Baz-Valle's no-extra-benefit was a soft ~12-20-set optimum for quads/biceps (triceps still gained beyond 20). The fixed MRV numbers are practitioner recovery heuristics (RP/Israetel, lower-tier), not trained RCTs. Effect vs practical: extra weekly sets show diminishing returns and rising fatigue/time cost (a real reason to cap volume), but 'additional sets stop producing ANY growth and become wasted' is not established at the weekly level.
population: trained and untrained young men predominantly; MRV landmarks generalized by practitioners to lifters of varying experience

statement: Higher training frequency produces more muscle growth (and more strength) than lower frequency: training a muscle 3-6x/week beats 1-2x/week.
nuance: All three lenses refute the independent-frequency growth claim (strength 0.82-0.85), but the honest finding is matched-volume equivalence for hypertrophy above ~2x/week -- frequency acts mainly as a volume vehicle -- so the directed verdict is equivalent. When weekly volume is held constant, frequency has negligible independent effect on hypertrophy (Pelland 2026 frequency-hypertrophy slope 'compatible with negligible effects'; Grgic 2018 volume-equated subgroup no strength effect, p=0.421, frequency effects 'primarily driven by volume'; SBS direct-measure hypertrophy differences trivial). The one robust floor is Schoenfeld 2016: >=2x/week beats 1x for growth, but 3x vs 2x and higher is undetermined. For STRENGTH a small genuine volume-matched benefit survives (Pelland posterior 100% but with strong diminishing returns; SBS ~20% faster, concentrated in upper-body pressing). Effect vs practical: higher frequency is valuable as a vehicle to add and distribute volume (lower per-session fatigue, higher per-set quality), not as an independent growth driver. The sweeping '3-6x beats 1-2x' conflates 'frequency lets you do more volume' (true) with 'frequency itself grows more at equal volume' (largely false for hypertrophy).
population: Healthy young/non-elderly adults, predominantly untrained-to-intermediate trained men; fewer data in highly trained lifters; both sexes (frequency-strength effect somewhat larger in women and in untrained).

statement: Training sets to momentary muscular failure is required to maximize muscle hypertrophy and strength; stopping short of failure leaves gains on the table.
nuance: Two lenses refute (strength 0.88-0.90) and one survives BECAUSE the refutation rests on measured outcomes, not a proxy -- net the falsifiable word 'required' is contradicted. Volume-equated evidence: Grgic 2022 meta (15 studies) found no significant failure-vs-non-failure difference for strength (ES=-0.09) or hypertrophy (ES=0.22, NS), with the volume-equated strength subgroup essentially zero (ES=0.01); Robinson 2024 meta-regression found strength similar across a wide RIR range; and trained-subject RCTs (Ruple 2023 0-1 vs 4-6 RIR; Martikainen 2025; Pelland/Robinson 2025) show similar strength and hypertrophy stopping short of failure. Effect vs practical: a genuine kernel survives -- you must train reasonably CLOSE to failure (hypertrophy rises as RIR falls; non-failure underperforms mainly when volume isn't equated), and failure 'idiot-proofs' effort since lifters underestimate proximity. But 'required to maximize' and 'short of failure leaves gains on the table' overstate: ~1-3 RIR matches growth and for strength failure is not beneficial and may mildly impair RFD. Caveat: a small trained-subgroup hint (ES=0.15) that failure modestly aids hypertrophy keeps this short of clean equivalence but does not rescue 'required.'
population: Young healthy adults (untrained and trained); moderate-to-high loads (60-90% 1RM). Failure may matter more at very low loads (~30% 1RM) and possibly slightly more for hypertrophy in well-trained lifters; data sparse in older/highly elite populations.

statement: Training to 0 RIR (failure) produces meaningfully more hypertrophy than training at 1-3 RIR; the closer to failure you stop, the more you grow, so 0 RIR beats leaving any reps in reserve.
nuance: Lenses split (2 refute the threshold at 0.75-0.80, 1 survives at 0.20) because the claim has a partially-supported continuous component and a refuted threshold component, all measured on actual muscle size. Supported part: Robinson 2024 meta-regression found a negative RIR-hypertrophy slope whose CI excluded null, so 'closer to failure = somewhat more growth' has meta-regression support for hypertrophy (notably NOT for strength, where the slope was null/possibly favoring leaving reps). Refuted part (the threshold '0 RIR meaningfully beats 1-3 RIR'): the curve flattens -- most benefit is captured by ~1-3 RIR -- and Henselmans/Nuckols note the steep near-failure slope may be a between-study volume-control artifact; the published Refalo meta found no evidence failure beats non-failure for hypertrophy. Trained-subject RCTs contradict 0-RIR superiority: Robinson IUSCA 2025 found 0-RIR/0-3-RIR slightly inferior for strength and unclear for hypertrophy; Martikainen 2025 and Ruple 2023 found similar hypertrophy with no 0-RIR advantage; for strength 0 RIR is same-or-worse. Effect vs practical: 1-3 RIR delivers nearly the full hypertrophy stimulus at much lower fatigue/RPE cost, making it the better risk-adjusted choice.
population: Young healthy resistance-trained men and women, moderate loads; hypertrophy trend strongest from RIR data on direct-measure outcomes; strength conclusions robust across trained samples. RIR-estimation accuracy is acceptable in trained lifters, which underpins applying these to real programs.

statement: Heavy loads (>~60-65% 1RM, low reps) are required to maximize muscle hypertrophy; light loads / high reps grow much less muscle because they fail to recruit and stimulate high-threshold motor units.
nuance: All three lenses refute (strength 0.85-0.93). When sets are taken to or near failure (effort-equated), hypertrophy is largely LOAD-INDEPENDENT across ~30-85% 1RM: Lopez 2021 network meta-analysis (28 studies, n=747, all to failure) found no hypertrophy difference between low/moderate/high loads (P=0.113-0.469, I2=0%); Grgic & Schoenfeld 2020 fiber-type meta found no difference for type I or type II fibers; Currier 2023 BJSM Bayesian NMA (119 studies) concluded 'all prescriptions comparably promoted muscle hypertrophy.' The stated MECHANISM is specifically falsified: by Henneman's size principle a low-load set carried to failure progressively recruits high-threshold motor units (Morton 2019 showed motor-unit activation unaffected by load at task failure), so HTMU recruitment is not heavy-load-exclusive -- the mechanism is a falsified proxy. Effect vs practical: the claim conflates strength with size -- strength IS load-dependent (Lopez high-vs-low SMD 0.60), but the claim asserts this for HYPERTROPHY, where it fails. Kernel of truth: growth is roughly halved near ~20% 1RM (a true lower bound) and light-load-to-failure is less time-efficient/more uncomfortable, so moderate-heavy loads are favored for efficiency/adherence, not growth magnitude.
population: healthy untrained-to-recreationally-trained adults; sets taken to or near failure; lower-body biopsy data predominate (limited upper-body and elite-athlete data)

statement: Standing (knee-extended) calf raises grow the gastrocnemius more than seated (knee-flexed) calf raises, because the biarticular gastrocnemius is trained at a longer muscle length when the knee is straight; the soleus grows similarly either way.
nuance: This is a genuine more-growth finding, not a false-equivalence. The growth half rests on a direct 12-week within-person MRI hypertrophy trial (Kinoshita 2023) that was both load-matched (70% 1RM) and volume/set-rep matched: standing (knee-extended) calf raises grew the gastrocnemius far more than seated (lateral +12.4% vs +1.7%, medial +9.2% vs +0.6%, d=1.53-1.58), while soleus grew similarly regardless of knee angle (+2.1% vs +2.9%, ns) -- so both halves of the claim are confirmed on a measured outcome, with the long-muscle-length mechanism corroborated by (not substituted for) the growth result. The single dissenting lens does not refute the effect direction; it flags external validity: the basis is a single uncontrolled study in n=14 untrained adults, so generalization to trained lifters is the only real weakness, and the operative variable is muscle length rather than knee position per se. Practical truth: train the gastroc with a straight knee (standing/leg-press calf raise) and the soleus with a bent knee (seated) -- the claim holds as stated, with confidence below 1.0 due to the thin, untrained evidence base.
population: untrained adults (within-person 12-wk MRI intervention); mechanism from biomechanics

statement: Longer rest intervals (~3 minutes) produce more muscle hypertrophy than short rest (~1 minute); short rest periods compromise growth.
nuance: The honest finding is volume-dependent equivalence at the growth ceiling, so the categorical 'short rest compromises growth' is an overstatement. There IS a real per-matched-sets effect: longer rest (>=2 min) produces somewhat more hypertrophy than short rest (~1 min) per equal number of sets, from an actual hypertrophy RCT (Schoenfeld 2016, trained men) plus practitioner meta-syntheses, with the plausible mechanism being central fatigue suppressing motor-unit recruitment and per-set load on compounds. But Krieger's meta-regression shows that per-set deficit is FULLY compensable by doing roughly double the sets, so maximal achievable growth is about the same with short or long rest -- the volume simply shifts (e.g., ~6-8 to ~15-16 sets/session). Lenses split (1 survives, 2 refute the strong wording), but they agree on the net: equal growth, not a categorical penalty. The MPS/central-fatigue mechanism row is not load-bearing for the verdict. Practical truth: rest longer for time-efficiency (fewer sets for the same growth) and to hold load/technique on heavy compounds -- not because short rest caps growth. Evidence base for the dedicated rest comparison is thinner/lower-tier than for load or volume.
population: resistance-trained and untrained young men; effect most pronounced on multi-joint/compound lifts; isolation lifts tolerate shorter rests better

statement: Periodized resistance training is superior to non-periodized training for strength (and hypertrophy) even when total volume and intensity are matched; planned systematic variation (e.g., DUP/linear) outperforms a constant program of equal workload.
nuance: The 'superior even when volume AND intensity are matched' clause is the weak point and is largely undercut. For STRENGTH there is meta-analytic support that periodized beats non-periodized (Williams 2017, ES=0.43; SBS ~22% faster, larger in trained), and that outcome rests on measured 1RM, not a proxy -- so one lens survives. But two strong critiques bite: (1) the Afonso 2019 umbrella review shows the pooled studies compared periodized vs CONSTANT programs (not vs non-periodized VARIED programs), and several were not matched at all (different volume/supervision), so the evidence supports VARIATION rather than periodization per se; (2) the strength edge is largely a peak-intensity/1RM-specificity confound -- the one study matching volume, average AND peak intensity found NO strength difference. For HYPERTROPHY the honest finding is equivalence when volume is equated (Grgic LP-vs-DUP meta, SBS). Lenses net to refuted on the matched-condition superiority while granting a modest, plausible benefit of variation. Practical truth: planned variation is reasonable to manage fatigue, mitigate the repeated-bout effect, and peak for competition, but 'outperforms an equal-workload constant program at matched volume and intensity, for strength AND hypertrophy' is not established and is contradicted for hypertrophy. Trained, long-duration, peak-intensity-matched data are sparse.
population: mostly untrained-to-recreationally-trained young adults, strength as primary outcome; short studies (6-16 wk); little data on highly-trained lifters or long-term/hypertrophy-primary designs

statement: The incline barbell/dumbbell press preferentially biases (and preferentially grows) the clavicular/upper head of the pectoralis major relative to the flat bench press, because the inclined arm path shifts mechanical and neural emphasis to the upper pec fascicles.
nuance: All three lenses flag the same fatal gap: the GROWTH half ('preferentially GROWS the clavicular head') rests on a proxy, not a direct outcome. The cited corpus contains NO flat-vs-incline trained-subject hypertrophy study -- the two provided sources (a biceps shoulder-position EMG paper and thorax anatomy texts) support only the general joint-angle-changes-activation mechanism. The biasing/ACTIVATION half is better grounded: the pectoralis major is regionally partitioned, and regional EMG (Cabral 2022, plus broader Rodriguez-Ridao 2020) shows inclining shifts excitation toward the upper/clavicular fascicles, which is why this is less wrong than the lat-grip claim. But activation predicts, it does not equal, regional hypertrophy. The one direct incline-hypertrophy data point (Chaves, single upper-site thickness, untrained) is modest and is not even cited. Effect-vs-practical: incline is a defensible tool to emphasize the upper chest, but the affirmative growth-superiority claim lacks the trained-RCT support it needs, and flat bench still trains the clavicular head substantially. Source_ids should be upgraded to a direct flat-vs-incline EMG/hypertrophy paper. Disputed: the direction is plausible and activation-supported, but the growth claim rests on mechanism/proxy and out-of-corpus work.
population: resistance-trained men (regional EMG); modest direct hypertrophy evidence (external)

statement: The barbell hip thrust produces greater gluteus maximus activation than the back squat and is therefore the superior exercise for growing the glutes.
nuance: All three lenses converge on a textbook EMG-to-growth leap. The activation premise is true: the barbell hip thrust elicits higher gluteus maximus surface EMG than the back squat (Contreras 2015, n=13 trained women, ~10RM: mean upper GMax 69.5% vs 29.4%; Neto 2020 review ~75% vs ~53% MVIC). But the 'therefore superior for growing the glutes' conclusion does not follow: (1) acute surface EMG does not reliably predict chronic hypertrophy -- Contreras 2015 itself calls for longitudinal studies and Neto flags EMG misinterpretation; (2) the corpus has NO volume-/effort-equated hypertrophy trial showing the hip thrust grows glutes more, and matched-volume RCTs in the broader literature show similar growth with region-specific biases; (3) the hip thrust is not even the highest-EMG glute exercise (step-ups exceed both). Practical truth: the hip thrust is an excellent, possibly preferable glute exercise for practical reasons (high tension at short muscle lengths, low spinal/systemic fatigue, easy to load and progress), but it is not established as superior for glute hypertrophy. The growth-superiority conclusion is refuted; the activation premise stands.
population: Resistance-trained adults (EMG data largely in trained women; activation review pooled trained men and women); hypertrophy comparison evidence sparse/absent in corpus

statement: The rectus femoris is hard to target/develop because, as a biarticular muscle, it suffers active insufficiency: it cannot be fully activated for knee extension when the hip is flexed (e.g., seated leg extension), so much of the muscle (especially the distal region) is never strongly recruited in common quad exercises.
nuance: The claim mixes a real phenomenon with a load-bearing mechanistic detail that the cited literature contradicts. SUPPORTED: the rectus femoris is biarticular and does exhibit active insufficiency in the length-tension sense -- it is a weaker knee extensor when the hip is flexed/shortened (StatPearls), and Miyamoto 2012 confirms task-dependent, regional control. REFUTED (the falsifiable core): the assertion that 'the distal region is never strongly recruited in common quad exercises' is backwards. Miyamoto plus direct knee-extension training studies (Narici, Blazevich) show the distal/middle RF preferentially contributes to KNEE EXTENSION and grows MORE distally from knee-extension training -- so in seated leg extension the distal RF is exactly the region that IS strongly driven; it is the PROXIMAL region biased to hip flexion that under-activates. Lenses split on framing: the volume-equation lens correctly notes this is a negative trainability/mechanism claim rather than a superiority claim (so that lens doesn't bite), while the anatomy-focused lenses refute the backwards distal-recruitment detail. The grain of truth: because RF crosses the hip, its overall knee-extension contribution is partly blunted when the hip is flexed, favoring less-hip-flexed positions for fuller stimulus. Practical takeaway (train RF in more hip-extended positions; it may lag with hip-flexed-only work) is defensible; the stated mechanism is not. Disputed.
population: Healthy adults (Miyamoto: 12 untrained/moderately active men, isometric MVC; HDEMG review synthesizes mixed healthy cohorts); training-hypertrophy inferences from knee-extension RCTs

statement: Reverse-pyramid training (heaviest top set first, then load drops) builds more muscle than equal-volume straight sets.
nuance: The claim explicitly invokes 'equal-volume straight sets' yet is refuted exactly where volume is matched, so the honest finding is no meaningful difference. The volume-equated within-subject RCT in well-trained men (Angleri 2017) found crescent pyramid produced statistically identical muscle CSA (7.5% vs 7.6%), 1RM, pennation, and fascicle-length gains as traditional straight sets, and the Fonseca 2023 meta (advanced paradigms incl. pyramid, GRADE moderate, I2=0%) found SMD ~ -0.00. All three lenses refute the 'more muscle' superiority: there is no supporting hypertrophy outcome, so the claim rests only on a loading-organization rationale, and the actual drivers (volume, load, proximity to failure) are supplied equally by straight sets. Caveat: no RCT in the corpus specifically tests a 'reverse' (descending) pyramid for hypertrophy, so this is equivalent-by-extension from crescent-pyramid and pooled advanced-technique data rather than flatly refuted on a reverse-pyramid trial. Practical truth: reverse pyramid is a legitimate, time-efficient, autoregulatory way to organize loading (fresh heavy top set, then lighter back-offs) that may suit some lifters, but it does not add hypertrophy over equal-volume straight sets.
population: Resistance-trained and recreationally trained adults (Angleri: well-trained men; Fonseca meta: recreationally/previously trained individuals)

statement: Pyramid training (varying load and reps across sets within one exercise) is superior to traditional straight sets for hypertrophy and strength.
nuance: The honest finding is parity, not superiority, on both outcomes, so the claim conflates 'at-par' with 'superior.' HYPERTROPHY: equivalent -- the volume-equated within-subject RCT (Angleri 2017, well-trained men) found crescent pyramid matched straight sets for CSA and muscle architecture, and the Fonseca 2023 meta (GRADE moderate, I2=0%) found no difference for advanced paradigms incl. pyramid (SMD ~ 0). STRENGTH: equivalent at best, and if anything traditional straight sets may be mildly preferable for pure strength because pyramid accumulates more fatigue from load/rep variation (Angleri found identical 1RM; the Cardozo/SBS review notes set structures allowing maximal force may be more optimal for strength). All three lenses refute the superiority framing on volume-equated outcome data. The 'covers multiple rep ranges/loads' benefit is a mechanism intuition already captured by volume, load, and proximity to failure -- it has no outcome backing as a magnitude-of-gains upgrade. Practical truth: pyramid is a viable, enjoyable way to add variety and naturally span loading zones, but it is not superior for hypertrophy or strength; the strength half tips slightly toward straight sets.
population: Resistance-trained and recreationally trained adults (Angleri: well-trained men; Fonseca meta: recreationally/previously trained); some pyramid data also in older adults

statement: Drop sets build more muscle than equal-volume straight sets.
nuance: The 'more muscle than equal-volume straight sets' claim is refuted by three independent meta-analyses converging on a null, including in volume-equated subgroups. Coleman 2022 (5 studies, 13 comparisons): hypertrophy ES=0.08 (95% CI -0.08 to 0.24), I2=0%. Sodal 2023: SMD=0.155 (p=0.392), falling to 0.08 when the non-equated study is removed. Havers 2026 (largest, 9 chronic studies, n=274): chronic SMD=0.04 (p=0.813), with the volume-equated subgroup SMD=-0.05 (ns) -- so equating volume does not reverse the null. All three lenses refute; the 'more muscle' wording survives only on a metabolic-fatigue/extra-stimulus proxy with no outcome support. Practical truth: the real, well-documented advantage is time-efficiency -- drop sets reach the same growth in roughly half-to-one-third of the training time (Fink ~145s vs ~316s; Ozaki ~2min vs ~7min) -- i.e. equal growth in less time, not more growth. Secondary nuance: one within-subject study (Varovic) hints at added regional rectus-femoris hypertrophy, and drop sets acutely raise RPE/lactate (higher fatigue cost). Reporting 'equal growth, less time' as 'more muscle' is the exact conflation this claim commits.
population: healthy adults, mostly resistance-trained young men (some untrained; single-joint/upper- and lower-body); 6-12 wk interventions

statement: Rest-pause and myo-rep training grow more muscle per unit of training time than traditional straight sets.
nuance: The claim must be split, and all three lenses refute the growth-superiority prong while granting the efficiency framing. ABSOLUTE GROWTH: equivalence, not superiority -- total hypertrophy from rest-pause/myo-reps matches straight sets when volume/effort are matched (Schwarz 2024 myo-rep thesis: 'comparable' adaptations; Fonseca 2023 SMD=-0.00; Tsartsapakis 2026 pooled g=0.046, p=0.370 ns -- though rest-pause was the single method with a small significant positive coefficient, a cautious signal on thin data). The lone longitudinal rest-pause growth edge (Prestes, thigh +11% vs +1%) is effort-confounded (the rest-pause group did more reps than the TRAD group's prescribed 6). PER-UNIT-TIME (efficiency): defensible -- these methods deliver comparable growth in markedly less time (Iversen 2021: roughly half the training time at maintained volume; Prestes 35 vs 57 min/session). The growth-superiority component fails because longitudinal evidence is sparse (essentially one rest-pause RCT, n=8 myo-rep thesis), confounded, and 'per unit of time' is rarely the metric studies actually equate. Net: 'equal growth in less time' is well supported; 'grows MORE muscle' is not -- disputed.
population: recreationally/resistance-trained young adults (rest-pause RCTs and a small n=8 myo-rep thesis); 6-8 wk; limited longitudinal data

statement: Squatting to a deep range of motion (at or below parallel, full knee flexion) builds more quadriceps and overall leg muscle than partial/shallow squats.
nuance: This is one of the few depth claims with longitudinal growth/strength data rather than just activation, which is why one lens accepts it as supported: chronic training studies (Bloomquist 2013, Kubo 2019, Bazyler 2014) and the SBS squat guide indicate deeper squats (or a mix of ranges) induce the most substantial functional and muscular gains, via longer muscle length and greater knee-extension demand at the bottom, and the lean explicitly discounts the muddy/reversed EMG. But two lenses bite on validity: (1) the underpinning studies are predominantly in untrained/recreational lifters, with 'deep' rarely meaning true end-ROM, so the effect is not established for trained populations; (2) the cited deep-vs-partial squat studies are load-matched but not work/tension-equated -- deeper ROM does more mechanical work per rep -- so part of the edge is a work-volume confound, and the acute EMG even reverses when load is equated (Da Silva: partial squats produced HIGHER GMax EMG when load was equated). Lenses split (1 supported, 2 refute on population/work-confound), and the effect direction has real outcome backing rather than resting on a proxy. Practical truth: train squats through a full, deep ROM for greater quad and overall leg growth -- the direction is sound, but the magnitude is partly a per-rep-work effect and the trained-population evidence is thin. Disputed.
population: untrained-to-recreationally-trained adults; mechanistically generalizes to trained but fewer direct trained-lifter trials

statement: The hip thrust biases the glutes toward their shortened/peak-contracted length while the squat (and deep hip hinges) load the glutes at a long/stretched length, so the two are complementary rather than redundant for complete glute development.
nuance: The short-length (hip thrust, peak contraction at full hip extension) vs long-length (squat/RDL, glute stretched at deep hip flexion) contrast is anatomically real and a sound programming rationale for complementary coverage. But the claimed payoff (combining the two yields MORE/complete glute development than doing more of either alone) is mechanism plus borrowed within-person length studies, with no head-to-head trial demonstrating an additive growth benefit. One lens accepts it as a complementarity principle (the lean itself declines to claim a quantified additive growth advantage); two lenses flag it as proxy/leverage reasoning. Honest finding: defensible as a complementary-coverage heuristic, NOT as a proven extra-growth claim. This is the constructive flip-side of the refuted 'hip thrust grows glutes more' claim: the hip thrust's value is the short-length emphasis it adds, not superior total growth.
population: trained lifters; mechanistic + practitioner consensus

statement: The barbell hip thrust grows the glutes more than the squat because it produces far greater gluteus maximus EMG/peak-contraction loading.
nuance: Textbook activation-does-not-equal-growth case, and all three lenses refute it. The claim rests on Contreras 2015 showing the hip thrust elicits ~2x the mean/peak gluteus maximus EMG of the back squat, but that paper itself disclaims hypertrophy inference and calls for longitudinal study. When the growth study arrived (Plotkin et al. 2023), squats and hip thrusts produced broadly SIMILAR glute hypertrophy and the larger hip-thrust EMG did not translate into more growth (acute proxy r ~ -0.03 to 0.5). Mechanistically the squat loads the glute at a longer muscle length (deep hip flexion), favoring it for growth, so if anything the squat edges it. Honest finding: roughly EQUIVALENT glute growth (squat arguably ahead) — both belong in a program; the hip thrust does not replace the squat. The strength-0.85 caveat (Contreras is 13 trained women; Plotkin is untrained, 9 weeks) means the equivalence rests on limited longitudinal data, but the EMG-superiority basis of the claim is directly contradicted.
population: trained women (EMG); trained/recreational adults (Plotkin growth study)

statement: A knee-dominant squat style (sitting straight down, more knee flexion ROM) builds quads better than a hip-dominant 'sit-back' style that shifts load to the hips.
nuance: All three lenses decline to certify this as 'supported,' but on evidence-grade rather than contradicting data: there is NO head-to-head sit-down-vs-sit-back hypertrophy trial in any population. The claim rests on coaching observation (SBS: lifters with strong deadlifts but 'chicken legs' improve when they sit down and train quads through more knee-flexion ROM) plus the well-supported general longer-ROM/longer-muscle-length growth principle applied to the quads. Biomechanically, summed knee+hip extensor demand at a given femur angle is fixed, but a knee-dominant pattern keeps the quads loaded through more knee-flexion ROM (longer quad length), which is a legitimate growth-relevant mechanism. Honest finding: a defensible within-quad emphasis heuristic, not a measured growth-superiority result, and not a claim that one style grows more total leg muscle. Disputed because it leans on mechanism/coaching wisdom rather than a direct outcome trial.
population: trained lifters (coaching/biomechanical inference); supported by longer-ROM growth principle

statement: Doing leg extensions with the hips more extended (reclined, ~40° vs 90° hip flexion) substantially increases rectus femoris growth without compromising vastus lateralis growth.
nuance: Two lenses pass it; one objects only on population/replication grounds, so it survives. It is backed by a direct within-participant MRI growth study (Larsen et al. 2024): identical leg-extension training at ~40 deg vs 90 deg hip flexion (volume- and effort-equated) produced ~50-170% MORE rectus femoris hypertrophy in the extended-hip (lengthened biarticular RF) condition, while monoarticular vastus lateralis growth was equal — both halves of the claim confirmed by an actual outcome, not activation. Honest caveats the recorded truth demands: (1) the RF benefit was LARGER proximally than distally, somewhat at odds with the usual lengthened-training pattern, and the mechanism is unclear; (2) it is a single study in ~22 untrained participants with no trained-subject replication; (3) exercises that lengthen the RF even more (reverse Nordic, sissy squat) may beat the leg extension for that muscle. So this is a confirmed within-exercise improvement, not necessarily the best RF exercise overall.
population: untrained adults (within-participant design)

statement: Foot position on the leg press (high/wide = more glute/hamstring; low/narrow = more quad) lets you bias which muscles the exercise trains.
nuance: All three lenses refute, unanimously, on the same grounds: this near-universal gym claim is mechanism/EMG only, with explicitly NO longitudinal hypertrophy study in the corpus comparing leg-press foot positions in any population. The biomechanical logic is sound — a high/wide placement increases hip-flexion ROM and hip-extensor (glute/ham) demand while reducing knee ROM; a low/narrow placement does the reverse, lengthening the quad's knee-flexion ROM — but summed knee+hip extensor demand at a given joint configuration is fixed, so foot position REDISTRIBUTES ROM and leverage rather than adding net stimulus, and EMG/leverage is not proof of differential growth. The quad-biasing direction (low foot = longer quad ROM) is more defensible than the glute/ham-biasing direction because it rides the supported longer-length principle. Honest finding: a reasonable directional heuristic, but the muscle-reallocation claim is unproven for growth.
population: general trainees; mechanistic/EMG inference

statement: Across lower-body muscles, training (or biasing partials) toward the lengthened/stretched position generally produces somewhat more growth than shorter-length training, and you should pick exercises that load the target muscle at long lengths.
nuance: Two lenses pass it; one objects on population grounds, so it survives as a hedged heuristic. The general longer-muscle-length growth advantage is grounded in actual volume-equated, failure-matched hypertrophy trials and a meta sub-group (Kassiano, Maeo, Pedrosa; ~+6.8% CSA vs full ROM, individual studies up to ~2x in calves/hip extensors), via greater fascicle-length and modest pennation gains — an outcome-based, appropriately hedged ('somewhat more') heuristic, not EMG. Critical nuances the recorded truth insists on: (1) it is almost certainly NOT 'stretch-mediated hypertrophy' — the mechanism is unresolved; (2) you do NOT need end-ROM or a deep-stretch feeling to benefit; (3) EMG/pump do NOT reliably predict which exercise grows a muscle more, so apply this via ROM/leverage, not activation; (4) magnitude is MODEST and the meta sub-group is only ~three studies, conducted largely in untrained lifters with possible attenuation in trained populations. Supported as a real, qualified growth heuristic explicitly distinguished from the over-claimed 'stretch-mediated' framing.
population: mostly untrained/recreational; some trained data; broad meta-analytic base

statement: Increasing the stretch/ROM of a hip hinge — e.g., a deficit or step Romanian deadlift, or pulling to a deeper stretch — increases posterior-chain stimulus and hamstring/glute growth versus a shorter-ROM version.
nuance: All three lenses refute, though they agree the longer-length DIRECTION is plausible. The step/deficit-RDL-specific evidence is acute EMG (Coratella: step-RDL increased excitation of GMax, semitendinosus, and erector spinae vs standard and stiff-leg RDL) — activation, not growth. The growth-level backing is BORROWED from a different movement: Maeo's lengthened-partial hip-extension MRI study (training the 90-45 deg lengthened range grew hip extensors ~2x more than full ROM), in untrained subjects. No trained-subject RCT directly tests deficit/step RDL vs standard RDL for hamstring/glute hypertrophy, so the named comparison's advantage is extrapolated from the general longer-length principle plus exercise-specific EMG, not directly measured. Honest finding: the longer-ROM-grows-more direction is corroborated by hypertrophy trials on OTHER movements, so it is a well-reasoned heuristic, but the specific step/deficit-RDL superiority is proxy + extrapolation. Practical cap: erector-spinae fatigue limits usable extra hinge ROM.
population: competitive bodybuilders (EMG); untrained/recreational (growth studies)

statement: Hip-hinge movements (RDL, stiff-leg deadlift, good morning) emphasize the hip-extensor hamstrings (biceps femoris long head, semimembranosus) plus glutes, while leg curls emphasize the knee-flexor hamstrings (semitendinosus, distal/short-head biceps femoris) — so both movement patterns are needed for complete hamstring development.
nuance: The strongest hamstring regional-bias claim: two lenses pass it and one objects only on trained-population grounds. The recruitment split is corroborated by BOTH consistent EMG region-mapping AND direct growth data, not EMG alone. The hamstring-glute regional EMG paper shows hip-hinge/hip-extension exercises (RDL, hip extension, step-up) drive GMax plus proximal/long-head biceps femoris and semimembranosus, while knee-flexion exercises (Nordic, leg curl) preferentially recruit semitendinosus and distal/medial biceps femoris (leg curl elicited the lowest GMax of six exercises). Crucially the split tracks each head's actual joint function (hip vs knee), and the growth pattern matches: Maeo's seated (hip-flexed, hip-extensors lengthened) leg curl grew the hip-extensor heads more, and lengthened hip-hinge training grew GMax/semimembranosus/semitendinosus/BF-long-head ~2x more than shortened. The dissenting lens notes the confirming Maeo work is untrained within-person MRI and the recruitment data are acute EMG (no trained-subject hypertrophy RCT), a fair population caveat. Honest finding: functionally coherent and growth-corroborated — program both a hip hinge and a leg curl.
population: trained men and women; growth study (Maeo) in untrained/recreationally trained

statement: The seated leg curl grows the hamstrings more than the lying/prone leg curl because the flexed-hip seated position trains the hip-extensor hamstring heads at a longer muscle length.
nuance: Two lenses pass it strongly; one objects only on population grounds. Backed by a direct within-participant MRI hypertrophy study (Maeo et al. 2021/2022), the gold standard for this comparison — not EMG. Because three of the four hamstring muscles are hip extensors, they are more lengthened in the flexed-hip seated position, and the seated leg curl produced GREATER hypertrophy of those hip-extensor heads than the lying/prone curl. The pattern is internally validated: the sartorius (a hip flexor, more lengthened in the lying curl) grew more there, confirming the 'every muscle trained at a longer length grew more' rule. The dissenting lens fairly notes it is a single within-person trial in participants without reported training experience, volume-/effort-equated but lacking a trained-subject replication. Honest finding: a real, directly measured growth advantage for the seated curl on the hip-extensor heads — modest in absolute terms, which is why RP still programs both seated and lying/standing variants across a week.
population: untrained/recreationally trained adults (within-person MRI design)

statement: Squat stance width changes the muscle bias: a wide stance shifts emphasis to the glutes/adductors, while a narrow stance emphasizes the quads.
nuance: All three lenses refute, unanimously and for the same reason: the wide-vs-narrow stance 'glute vs quad' reallocation rests almost entirely on acute EMG and biomechanics (Paoli 2009: larger stance widths yield greater GMax EMG and more hip-flexion/adductor involvement) with NO longitudinal hypertrophy trial comparing stances in any population. SBS's squat guide stresses that total summed knee+hip extensor demand at a given depth is identical regardless of stance — stance changes how demand is DISTRIBUTED, not the total — and EMG is a poor predictor of regional growth. The one defensible piece is the adductor magnus: its hip-extension contribution at depth is real and large, so a wider/deeper stance plausibly trains adductors more. But 'glute vs quad' growth reallocation is unproven. Honest finding: stance is mainly a comfort/depth/leverage decision; the muscle-bias claim leans on activation/mechanism with mixed practical evidence.
population: trained lifters; EMG studies in resistance-trained men and women

statement: Standing (knee-extended) calf raises grow the gastrocnemius far more than seated (knee-flexed) calf raises, while the soleus grows about equally either way — so standing biases the gastroc and seated is mainly needed to target the soleus.
nuance: Two lenses pass it cleanly (strength 0.05-0.10); one objects only on untrained-population grounds, so it survives strongly. Backed by a direct 12-week within-person MRI trial (Kinoshita et al. 2023) with identical reps/sets/load on both legs (70% 1RM, 10x5) — fully volume- and effort-equated. Standing (knee-extended, gastroc lengthened) produced far greater gastrocnemius growth than seated (knee-flexed, gastroc slack): lateral gastroc +12.4% vs +1.7%, medial +9.2% vs +0.6%, whole triceps surae +5.6% vs +2.1% (Cohen's d 0.88-1.58, large), with essentially NO significant gastroc growth in the seated condition. The monoarticular soleus, unaffected by knee angle, grew similarly in both (+2.1% vs +2.9%, trivial) — both halves of the claim confirmed by actual muscle-volume outcomes, not EMG, and it doubles as a clean longer-muscle-length result. The dissenting lens fairly notes it is a single trial in 14 untrained adults with no trained replication. Honest finding: standing builds the gastroc, seated is mainly needed to reach the soleus; 'seated also builds the gastroc' is effectively false.
population: untrained adults (within-person MRI design)

statement: Behind-the-neck overhead pressing is superior (e.g., for the delts) to front/military pressing.
nuance: All three lenses refute: the behind-the-neck-press superiority claim has ZERO outcome support. There is no hypertrophy or strength trial in any population showing behind-neck pressing beats front/military pressing, which loads the same prime movers (anterior + lateral deltoid) through a safer path; any delt-targeting benefit is activation/mechanism-level at best. Worse, the variation carries a worse risk profile — forcing maximal external rotation plus horizontal abduction increases subacromial/impingement and anterior-capsule stress, especially in lifters with limited shoulder mobility — so the added joint risk is not justified by any evidenced growth payoff. Honest finding: front and behind-neck pressing are at best EQUIVALENT for the delts, and the claim of behind-neck SUPERIORITY is unsupported (the original lean's rejection aligns with all three lenses).
population: General lifters; no direct growth comparison

statement: Cable lateral raises are superior to dumbbell lateral raises because the cable keeps tension on the side delt in the stretched/lengthened (bottom) position where dumbbells offer almost none.
nuance: All three lenses refute the growth-superiority claim: it rests entirely on a resistance-curve / tension-at-length mechanism (cables keep tension on the side delt in the stretched bottom position where dumbbells offer almost none), and the lean itself concedes there is NO cable-vs-dumbbell lateral-raise hypertrophy study. The lengthened-ROM advantage is extrapolated from other muscles / largely untrained data, not a trained-subject head-to-head growth trial. Effect vs practical: loading the stretched position is a sound mechanistic and exercise-selection rationale, and the broader stretch-hypertrophy literature mildly favors loading long muscle lengths, so cables are a reasonable choice for constant tension and a fuller resistance profile -- but 'superior for growing the side delt' is not demonstrated; at best the two are likely comparable for matched-volume growth, with cables offering a tension-profile edge that has not been shown to translate into more hypertrophy.
population: Mechanistic; extrapolated from lengthened-training literature

statement: Dips and decline pressing preferentially train/grow the lower (sternocostal/costal) pectoralis major.
nuance: All three lenses refute the GROWTH half. The lower-pec (sternocostal/costal) bias of dips and decline pressing is established only at the acute EMG level (Glass, Rodriguez-Ridao show greater costal-pec activation), but no longitudinal trial shows greater lower-pec growth than flat bench -- the only regional-pec growth trial (Chaves, untrained) studied flat vs incline and never tested decline or dips. Effect vs practical: the activation difference makes decline/dips a defensible tool to emphasize the lower/costal fibers, and the directional EMG evidence is real, so as exercise selection the heuristic is reasonable -- but the specific assertion that they preferentially GROW the lower pec is unsupported by any volume-equated hypertrophy study and rests on an activation proxy that does not reliably predict regional growth.
population: Trained men (EMG); no growth trial for decline/dips

statement: Acute EMG activation (or acute muscle swelling/pump) reliably predicts which exercise will cause more regional hypertrophy.
nuance: This is the foundational proxy claim, and the consensus is that it is false: acute EMG activation and acute muscle swelling/pump do NOT reliably predict which exercise drives more regional hypertrophy. Two lenses refute it outright and the third agrees the predictive value should be rejected (its refuted=false flag means the negative claim survives the lens, i.e. it too concludes EMG/swelling fails to predict growth). The equated/longitudinal evidence (Vigotsky; Plotkin/Albarello) shows EMG, swelling, and actual growth pointing in different directions with weak, sometimes near-zero or negative correlations (r ~ -0.03 to 0.5). Effect vs practical: activation and pump are useful for exercise familiarization and effort feedback, but as a tool to forecast regional growth they are unreliable; the honest finding decisively refutes the proxy-predicts-growth premise. Note much of the contrary data is in untrained, low-n samples, which is itself a reason not to lean on these proxies.
population: Trained lifters; applies across muscle groups

statement: Flat (horizontal) bench pressing biases the sternal/mid portion of the pectoralis major.
nuance: All three lenses refute the regional-GROWTH half (the lean had rated it 'supported'). The one volume-equated longitudinal trial (Chaves, untrained) found NO group difference at the mid/sternal pec sites (3rd and 5th intercostal NS), so flat pressing did not grow the mid-pec more than incline; the bias rests on acute EMG-change and acute swelling -- non-equated proxies for a pump, not a demonstrated hypertrophy edge -- in untrained subjects, which does not meet a trained-RCT bar. Effect vs practical: flat bench does load and activate the sternal/mid fibers well and is a sensible mid-chest staple, and the EMG direction is plausible, so the directional emphasis is fine for exercise selection -- but 'biases mid-pec GROWTH' overstates: the matched-volume data show parity, not a flat-bench advantage, at the mid-pec.
population: Trained and untrained young men

statement: Combining incline and flat pressing in the same program maximizes overall pectoralis growth/strength versus doing either alone.
nuance: The 'combine incline and flat to maximize pec growth' claim is directly contradicted by the only longitudinal trial in the corpus: in the volume-equated Chaves (2020) study the combination group did NOT maximize growth -- it grew the upper pec LESS than incline-only and merely matched flat for the mid-pec. Two lenses refute on this outcome; the third (refuted=false) agrees the maximization claim fails because it will not let an untrained, low-n study RESCUE a superiority claim. Effect vs practical: using multiple angles is still a reasonable way to distribute stimulus and hedge regional coverage, and the trial is single/untrained so it cannot prove combining is harmful -- but the specific assertion that combining MAXIMIZES growth versus doing either alone is refuted under matched volume, not supported.
population: Untrained young men, 8 weeks, 1x/week

statement: Incline pressing (around 30-45 degrees) biases the clavicular/upper head of the pectoralis major and grows the upper chest more than flat pressing.
nuance: The lenses split (1 survives, 2 refute). Unlike the other regional-bench claims, incline's upper-pec edge does have a volume-equated longitudinal finding behind it -- Chaves (2020) reported incline-only grew the 2nd-intercostal (upper) pec more than flat AND than the combination -- so it does not rest on EMG alone. But that support is a single small, untrained, once-weekly 8-week trial with only ~10/group for thickness and an implausible ~62% outlier the reviewers flag, the EMG at 0 vs 30 degrees was non-significant (p=0.688), and acute swelling data contradicted the direction. Effect vs practical: incline is a defensible, widely-endorsed tool to emphasize the clavicular/upper chest and the direction is plausible, so 'incline for upper pec' is reasonable exercise selection -- but the magnitude/certainty is weak; the upper-pec GROWTH advantage hangs on one thin outlier study and falls short of the trained-RCT evidence needed to call it firmly supported.
population: Trained and untrained young men (growth trial in untrained men; EMG in trained men)

statement: Lengthened-biased curls that load the stretched position (e.g., incline dumbbell curls) build the biceps more than shortened-position curls like preacher curls.
nuance: Only one lens refutes, and the claim is backed by an actual hypertrophy OUTCOME, so it survives. Two lenses note the lengthened-position curl advantage rests on volume-equated, failure-matched biceps-curl RCTs (stretched vs peak-contraction/shortened) and a meta sub-group showing about +6.8% more growth at long muscle lengths -- a measured growth difference, not an EMG or stretch-mediated mechanism proxy. The dissenting lens validly cautions that the biceps RCTs are 'nearly all in untrained participants,' the effects are modest, and the exact incline-curl-vs-preacher pairing is extrapolated rather than directly trialed. Effect vs practical: training the biceps in a lengthened position (e.g., incline curls) is a sound, evidence-aligned choice that tends to modestly out-grow shortened/peak-contraction work like preacher curls -- but the edge is small, partly extrapolated, and largely from untrained samples, so it is a meaningful emphasis rather than a large or guaranteed superiority.
population: Mostly untrained/recreational; some trained data; effect may shrink with training age

statement: Rows are a poor lat exercise because the lat loses leverage and tension at the top, and lat-focused work should emphasize long muscle lengths (e.g., straight-arm pull-overs / lat prayers).
nuance: All three lenses refute. The argument is a coherent moment-arm / length-tension mechanism (Henselmans: the lat has a near-zero moment arm overhead and loses leverage/tension at the top of a row), but it is acknowledged pure biomechanics -- there is explicitly NO head-to-head hypertrophy trial in any population showing pull-overs or lat prayers grow the lats more than rows or pulldowns. Effect vs practical: emphasizing long-length lat work (straight-arm pull-overs, lat prayers) is a reasonable exercise-selection heuristic and the leverage reasoning is internally consistent, so adding stretch-biased lat work is defensible -- but 'rows are a poor lat exercise' is a mechanism-only selection claim, not demonstrated by any equated growth comparison, and rows still load the lats substantially, so the dismissal of rows for lats is unsupported as a growth statement.
population: Mechanistic/EMG + moment-arm data; no human growth comparison

statement: Horizontal rows bias the mid-back (rhomboids/mid-trapezius) while vertical pulldowns bias the lats.
nuance: All three lenses refute the differential-GROWTH implication (the lean had rated it 'supported'). The rows-bias-mid-back / pulldowns-bias-lats split rests solely on Sperandei surface EMG (rows recruit mid-trap and rhomboids more), with no regional-growth trial; moreover that EMG used only ~30-40% MVC loads, so high-threshold fibers were not even fully recruited, weakening even the activation case. Effect vs practical: this is a broadly accepted directional pattern and a sensible programming heuristic -- horizontal rows do emphasize the mid-back musculature and vertical pulldowns the lats, so including both for complete back development is reasonable -- but an acute, low-intensity activation difference is not proof of differential hypertrophy. The honest finding is directional activation guidance, not demonstrated region-specific growth.
population: Trained men (EMG)

statement: A supinated (underhand) pulldown grip shifts work to the biceps while a pronated grip preferentially trains the lats/back.
nuance: The folk rule fails on its own terms: Sperandei found biceps AND latissimus activation statistically the SAME across pronated and supinated pulldown grips, so the 'underhand = arms, overhand = back' split has neither EMG nor any volume-equated growth support. Two lenses refute it; the third (refuted=false) agrees, noting this negative claim survives the lens precisely because the only proxy behind the popular rule found no difference. Effect vs practical: the honest finding is essentially no meaningful difference -- grip orientation on the pulldown does not measurably shift work from lats to biceps -- so grip can be chosen for comfort, wrist/elbow stress, and bar path rather than for regional targeting. The asserted bias is overstated and contradicted by the activation data, with no hypertrophy evidence to rescue it.
population: Trained men (EMG)

statement: A wide pronated grip on the lat pulldown preferentially recruits/grows the latissimus dorsi compared with a closer grip.
nuance: All three lenses refute. The wide-grip lat 'bias' rests on mixed, mostly non-significant acute EMG: Sperandei found only a small wide-grip edge the authors themselves said 'may have no weight training significance,' while Signorile favored wide -- an inconsistent activation picture -- and there is NO longitudinal study showing a wide pronated grip grows the lats more than a closer grip. Effect vs practical: grip width does change shoulder/elbow position, comfort, and which synergists are loaded, so varying grip is fine for those reasons, and a wide grip remains a perfectly good lat exercise -- but the specific claim that wide grip preferentially RECRUITS or GROWS the lats is unsupported, resting on an inconsistent acute-EMG edge with no trained-subject hypertrophy trial behind it. The honest finding is at best no reliable lat-growth advantage from grip width.
population: Trained men (EMG, isometric and 10-12RM dynamic)
